match.reason: The closest bank point, Linear functions, covers the point-gradient form y - y₁ = m(x - x₁) but not converting to the general form ax + by + c = 0, and it is pitched at Year 11 rather than Stage 5 paths, so no bank point teaches this full idea at the right depth.

draft.title: Point-gradient and general form
card: If a line has gradient \(m\) and passes through the point \((x_{1}, y_{1})\), its equation is \(y - y_{1} = m(x - x_{1})\). Put in the numbers, then tidy up.
Example: gradient \(3\), through \((2, 5)\). This gives \(y - 5 = 3(x - 2)\). Expanding gives \(y - 5 = 3x - 6\), so \(y = 3x - 1\).
General form writes the equation as \(ax + by + c = 0\), with everything on one side equal to zero. Usually \(a\), \(b\) and \(c\) are whole numbers.
To change \(y = 3x - 1\) to general form, move every term to one side: \(3x - y - 1 = 0\). To go back, make \(y\) the subject. Then the gradient is the number in front of \(x\).
draft.remember: Use \(y - y_{1} = m(x - x_{1})\) to build a line, then rearrange it to the form you need.

a.q: A line has gradient \(2\) and passes through \((1, 4)\). Which equation is correct?
a.why: The point \((1, 4)\) gives \(x_{1} = 1\) and \(y_{1} = 4\), so the equation is \(y - 4 = 2(x - 1)\). Swapping the coordinates, as in \(y - 1 = 2(x - 4)\), gives a line through \((4, 1)\) instead.
a.clue: The \(y\) value of the point goes with \(y\).

b.q: A line has gradient \(-2\) and passes through \((3, -1)\). What is its equation in general form?
b.why: The line is \(y + 1 = -2(x - 3)\), which expands to \(y + 1 = -2x + 6\). Moving everything to the left gives \(2x + y - 5 = 0\). Forgetting that \(y - (-1)\) is \(y + 1\) leads to \(2x + y - 7 = 0\).
b.clue: Subtracting \(-1\) is the same as adding \(1\).

problems.detail: The card says a, b and c are 'usually whole numbers', but its own example 3x - y - 1 = 0 has b = -1 and c = -1. In Australian usage 'whole numbers' means 0, 1, 2, …, so 'integers' would be accurate.

check.summary: Both answers and both explanations are correct. The only issue is that the card calls a, b and c 'whole numbers' when its own example uses negative values; 'integers' is the right word.
